title: 서울 여름: '나태함' 대신 '더위 탓'

📅 Updated 2026.08.04
Key takeaways
  • 서울의 여름은 살인적인 더위로 인해 누구나 무기력하고 의욕이 저하됩니다.
  • 이런 감정은 개인의 나약함이 아니라 더위 때문이니 스스로를 자책하지 마세요.
  • 작은 성취와 보상을 통해 버티고, 더위가 지나면 다시 활력을 찾을 수 있습니다.
👤 이 글은 한국의 여름을 겪어본, 또는 겪을 예정인 외국인들을 위한 글입니다. 특히 한국의 일상과 직장 생활에 관심 있는 분들이라면 공감하실 수 있을 겁니다.

Living in Seoul, especially during the summer, can feel like a constant battle against an invisible enemy. Lately, I keep hearing the same complaints from everyone around me: “Why am I so unmotivated?” “I really don’t want to do anything.” “I’m definitely not going outside.” It’s a chorus of negativity. Some friends even start criticizing themselves, calling themselves weak or lacking willpower. My wife and I, for example, started a diet two weeks ago, and with this brutal heatwave hitting us, we’re already on the verge of giving up. Again.

Let me be direct: Don’t blame yourself. And don’t try to fight this heat head-on. Honestly, it’s a losing battle.

It’s funny how many people don't seem to realize that the real reason they're feeling so drained and unmotivated, so disappointed in themselves, is simply the weather. This year’s summer has been particularly relentless. I can’t tell if it’s just me getting older and more susceptible to the heat, or if this oppressive summer is genuinely worse, affecting everyone from kids to seniors. Maybe I just lack the life wisdom to deal with it, who knows? All I know is, this summer’s heat is casting a much bigger shadow of negativity than I expected, not just on my friends and colleagues, but on what feels like most of the city.

The Seoul Summer Slump is a Legitimate Illness

When I say the heat is brutal, I mean it. We're talking about daily highs consistently above 30°C (86°F) with suffocating humidity that makes it feel much hotter. The air outside is thick and heavy, like a wet blanket. My morning commute on the subway, usually a packed but tolerable experience, becomes an ordeal. Even with the air conditioning blasting, the sheer number of bodies generates so much heat. By the time I get to the office, I feel like I've already run a marathon. This isn't just discomfort; it’s a fundamental drain on your energy. I’ve noticed people at my company, usually buzzing with `palli-palli` (hurry-hurry, do-it-now) energy, moving slower, talking less, and visibly wilting. It's not just big tasks; even mundane things like brushing your teeth or walking to the convenience store for lunch can feel like too much effort. Suddenly, the ambition to start something new, or even just maintain existing routines, collapses under the weight of the heat. That diet I mentioned? My wife, usually a disciplined person, broke down and ordered `jjajangmyeon` (black bean noodles) for herself, then immediately felt guilty. It’s a common story in this season.

Why We Blame Ourselves, and Why That's a Mistake

Koreans, generally speaking, are a pretty driven and self-critical bunch. We value hard work, perseverance, and often push ourselves to the limit. So when you find yourself struggling to even do the basics, it’s easy to internalize that failure. You might think, “Why am I so weak?” or “Everyone else seems fine, what’s wrong with me?” But trust me, that’s just the heat messing with your head. For months now, I’ve been putting off things I really want to do. I’ve had this blog post planned, along with a few other content ideas, for about two months. Every morning, I tell myself, “Today’s the day,” but by the time I get home from work, I’m utterly exhausted. My body feels like a rag doll. My brain is fried. I blame this monstrous summer for the delay, and honestly, it’s a legitimate excuse. Going to the gym? Forget about it. The thought of adding more physical exertion to my already heat-drained body is just unbearable. I get home and just want to collapse in front of the air conditioner. It’s a vicious cycle of wanting to do things, not having the energy, and then feeling guilty about it. But here’s the thing: it’s not a personal failing. It’s the environment.

Strategic Surrender: My Guide to Surviving Summer

So, what do you do when you feel this way? You can’t just stop living, obviously. For me, the answer is to practice a bit of strategic surrender. Instead of fighting the current, I try to ride it out. I’ve learned not to try and do too much. The key is to acknowledge the limitations the heat imposes and focus on just getting through the absolute essentials. I try to be proud of myself for simply making it through the workday, for sticking to my most basic routines. Anything beyond that is a bonus. The things I want to do – like writing this blog, or catching up on my reading – I tell myself I’ll get to them when the heat no longer has such a firm grip on me. There’s no rush. I just keep my daily routine going, one day at a time, without getting too anxious about grand plans.

My personality is naturally quite hard on myself, so this approach isn't easy. But it’s my way of trying to beat, or at least survive, the summer. I focus on a few non-negotiable routines that make me feel somewhat productive and satisfied: a bit of at-home exercise, reading a few pages of a book, maybe jotting down some ideas for content. That’s it. Anything else is gravy. And then, to combat the negativity and reward myself for simply enduring, I throw in little treats. A cold beer in front of the blasting air conditioner, for instance. Or ordering in my favorite takeout, instead of cooking in a hot kitchen. These small pleasures become lifelines.

Planning a Break to Reset and Recharge

I want to tell anyone reading this, especially if you’re struggling: it's perfectly okay if you're only managing to do the ‘must-dos’ right now. If you're really struggling, don't stress yourself out trying to be a superhero. Instead, give yourself a pat on the back. Seriously. You can blame your lazy self later, when the heat finally subsides, or when you’ve somehow managed to adapt to it. Until then, cut yourself some slack. If your mind is full of negative thoughts and things aren't going according to your will, it's because of this sudden, sweltering summer. It’s a temporary problem, and it will pass. So, in the meantime, try to enjoy the small moments you can.

As for me, I’ve found that I’ve adapted a little bit to the heat, and I’ve certainly come to understand my own limitations against it. So, this coming Wednesday, I've decided to use a `yeoncha` (annual leave day) to turn the tide on my own laziness. I’ve made a plan, and I'm genuinely excited about this new turning point. My lovely wife, who just ordered `jjajangmyeon` alone and then scolded herself for it, is also on board. We’re going to shake off this lethargy together, starting this week. The summer won’t defeat us entirely. We’ll just… wait for it to pass, with a strategic `yeoncha` in hand.

Questions people always ask

Q. 한국의 여름은 얼마나 더운가요?

A. 서울의 여름은 보통 7월 중순부터 8월 말까지 지속되며, 기온이 30°C를 꾸준히 넘고 습도가 매우 높아 체감 온도는 훨씬 높게 느껴집니다. '열대야' 현상으로 밤에도 기온이 25°C 이상을 유지하는 경우가 많습니다.

Q. 더위에 지쳤을 때 직장인들은 어떻게 대처하나요?

A. 저처럼 많은 직장인들이 퇴근 후 바로 집으로 가 에어컨 앞에서 휴식을 취하거나, 주말에는 실내 활동 위주로 계획을 세웁니다. `yeoncha` (연차, annual leave)를 사용해 잠시 쉬어가거나 재충전의 시간을 갖기도 합니다.

Q. 외국인들이 한국 여름에 가장 어려워하는 점은 무엇인가요?

A. 아마도 높은 습도와 에어컨이 없는 곳에서의 생활일 겁니다. 대중교통이나 실내 공간은 시원하지만, 짧은 거리라도 밖을 걷는 것이 매우 힘들고 불쾌할 수 있습니다.

Q. 여름철에 무기력해지는 것이 일반적인 현상인가요?

A. 네, 매우 일반적인 현상입니다. 많은 한국인들이 여름철에 에너지 저하와 집중력 감소를 경험하며, 이를 '여름 타는 것'이라고 표현하기도 합니다. 너무 자책하지 마세요.

Q. 한국 여름을 쾌적하게 보내기 위한 팁이 있다면?

A. 시원한 실내 활동 위주로 계획하고, 수분 섭취를 충분히 하며, 휴대용 선풍기나 쿨링 스프레이를 활용하는 것이 좋습니다. `patbingsu` (팥빙수, shaved ice dessert) 같은 시원한 디저트도 좋은 피서법입니다.

Where this comes from

  • 한국 기상청 (Korea Meteorological Administration)
